rv.q: Affection is the key that opens the show's comedy: You feel for Doug and Bud, and even root for them.
The only trigger warning required is one that cautions laughter ahead.
At first, all off the goings-on are entertaining in a crazy kind of way — until they become less and less so.
For the most part—thanks to its completely winning stars, and to the play’s own best stretches of joyful buffoonery—yes.

They are winning leading men — even as their antics on a bare-bones, brick-backed set (scenic design by Scott Pask) rarely surmount to much beyond a SNL sketch with the aftertaste of “follow your wildest dreams” inspiration.
With all of this pseudo-historical absurdity, Brown and King’s dotty comedy ultimately grounds itself in the likeability of its frontmen: Gad and Rannells.
But it’s not a 100% laugh riot either.
Even at a fairly pacey two hours the fun eventually turns to wheel-spinning, since the central gag is established from the start and then merely elaborated.
Here the problem is not excess but triteness; the tropes of sincere incompetence and pathetic ambition are too familiar, if expertly carried out.
Gad and Rannells are simply divine delivering a master class in musical comedy and likely setting a land/speed record for laughs per minute.

Thanks to these stars, if you head to the James Theater, you’ll laugh. You’ll wince. You may even tear up a bit. Above all, you’ll be incredibly impressed by the pair’s incredible chemistry as well as their go-for-broke mentality in selling this ridiculous material. Without question, Gad and Rannells absolutely earn an A+ for effort.
If you feel the need to laugh and let go, you can trust Andrew Rannells and Josh Gad, formerly stars of The Book of Mormon, to be your expert facilitators.
What makes it worth the visit is the time we get to spend with Bud and Doug.
I would have happily sat twice as long as that through a production of this quality.
The humor in Gutenberg! could stand to be a bit more like the rat-infested streets upon which the meta-show’s characters walk, and a certain nastiness could have elevated this from good to great.
Somehow the comedy gets drained during these asides and the show comes to a stop.
This fluffy, insider meta-musical for those who love musicals is nothing more than a diversion, mildly tweaking the conventions of Broadway and ribbing those who are obsessed with them.
The show is a roughly 2-hour sketch – one that’s clever and filled with laughs but too long and overstuffed to ward off diminishing returns.
In fact, there’s a bit of genius in their stupidity.

The problem is that the show they’ve supposedly devised is not particularly funny, with the relatively esoteric subject matter not exactly lending itself to riotous satire – even Mel Brooks would have trouble coming up with more than a few throwaway gags about Gutenberg.
There are some funny lines, but no more than an hour’s worth of laughs in a two-person vaudeville routine that goes on for two hours, becoming tedious.
It manages to waste the talent of not one but two very talented performers.
Gutenberg!, nimbly directed by Alex Timbers, is a blast from beginning to end.
Skillfully directed by Alex Timbers, “Gutenberg” is absurd, so don’t come for the story or expect to learn anything.
It’s difficult to watch performers work this hard when the humor isn’t exactly there in the source material.

cn.t: Critics are mixed on this meta-musical reunion of Gad and Rannells, praising the duo's effortless chemistry but finding the thin premise wears out over two hours. A lightweight, silly diversion that delights musical theater fans despite limited substance.

sg.ra: JEJ is one of Broadway's smallest houses (1,063-1,092 seats across sources) and seats 101-112 in Center Orch rows AA-A put you almost nose-to-stage; SeatPlan and Headout both name seats 105-109 in AA-A as the single best spots. Mezz overhang doesn't bite until Row J, so Center Orch stays clean of ceiling cutoff all the way back to Row I.

SeatPlan explicitly calls out 'Rows E to J in the Center Orchestra are cheaper than premium with a good view,' and because JEJ's auditorium is unusually compact even Row J sits closer to the stage than mid-orch in bigger Shubert houses. This is the sweet spot before the Mezz overhang obscures the top of the stage (SeatPlan: cuts in after Row O; TickPick: overhang begins Row J but worsens deeper).

sg.vl: Overview pick with an elevated head-on
sg.ra: JEJ Mezz is one of Broadway's smallest (264-275 seats) and sits directly above the stage per SeatPlan: 'every row facing directly above the stage.' SeatPlan notes the Balcony overhang at Mezz Row B 'doesn't affect views' and the railing height doesn't obstruct (TickPick). Good rake means heads-in-front is a non-issue. AVFMS April 2024: 'View was fantastic, person in front didn't obstruct my view.'

sg.vl: Underrated value if you skew center
sg.ra: Unusual for Broadway, TickPick explicitly states JEJ 'does not have obstructed view seats on the sides of the orchestra and mezzanine' thanks to the small footprint and no pillars. But SeatPlan warns double-digit seats at the far side and Boxes above 16 are angled with stage right partially obstructed, so you want the low-numbered seats closer to center aisle.
sg.rr: L Mezz A-G odd 1-25; R Mezz A-G even 2-26; plus 24 box seats

sg.vl: Cheapest tier, steepest price in comfort
sg.ra: SeatPlan: Balcony is 'very steep and cramped compared to the lower two seating areas,' ~2 steps down per row with three flights of stairs (Shubert: 55 steps total or elevator post-renovation). SeatPlan flags Row H as 'isn't as well-raked as the rest of the section,' so the back row both loses rake AND inherits the steep climb. JEJ balcony is unusually high — Shubert's own description puts it behind Row F entrance.
sg.rr: A-G (L/R) / A-H (Center); 283 seats plus 12 box seats

vr.q: that's where I think this two or three star material gets elevated into a four-star evening at the theater because they're both so wonderful in it
I did get a little tired of it after a while... I think I wanted more for the show to reach that next level comedy status, but I still found it super clever and enjoyable.
I don't think the material is particularly memorable. I mostly think it's just a decent vehicle for Josh Gad and Andrew Reynolds to be funny together on stage.
